description: Well-modelled Dart value types (domain primitives) for what is usually left as a raw String, int or double: email, IBAN, UUID, IP address, calendar dates and other ISO/RFC/GS1-standardised values, plus constraint types like Port and Percentage. Parse, don't validate: every instance is guaranteed well-formed.
rules: Parse, don't validate: no type has a public constructor, so a value that exists is guaranteed well-formed, the same guarantee `Uri` gives for URLs. Build one through the type's own door, never a constructor.

No door throws. `parse` returns a `ParseOutcome`: either the value, or a typed failure from that type's own vocabulary (`IbanFailure`, `DateFailure`, ...), so you can `switch` on the cause or read `.reasonOrNull` for a form-field message. `tryParse` is the same check returning `null`. The assembly factories (`fromComponents`, `fromBody`, `fromBytes`, `Date.of`) return that same `ParseOutcome`, so they do not throw either: append `.getOrThrow()` when you want to assert instead of branch. That is the one door that throws, and it raises `MintedFormatError`, an `Error` rather than an `Exception`, so `on FormatException` does not catch it.

Not every type parses text. Constraint types (`Digit`, `Digits`, `Port`, `Uint`, `NaturalNumber`, `Uint2` through `Uint32`, `Percentage`, `Probability`) take a `tryFrom` door over a number, or a `List<int>` on `Digits`, and deliberately have no `parse` / `tryParse`, because no standard defines a text form for a bare number: decode text yourself, as in `Digit.tryFrom(int.parse(text))`. Classifications (`Weekday`, `UuidVariant`, `PhoneNumberType`, `CardScheme`, `PortRange`, `Iso8601DurationComponent`) are enums a value type hands back, so they have no parse door either. `Month` is NOT one of these: it is a value type and does parse.

Single-primitive types are zero-cost extension types over that primitive: `Email` over String, `Port` over int, `Percentage` over double. Types with parts worth naming (`GeoCoordinate`, `Cidr`, `PaymentCardNumber`, `Digits`) are immutable classes. Both give value equality and hashCode. The canonical form reads back from `.value`, except on `Digits`, where it is `.asString`: a `Digits` interpolates as `Digits(978)` rather than `978`, which matters for the digit getters `Isbn.prefix`, `Isbn.body`, `Imei.tac`, `Imei.reportingBodyIdentifier` and `Imei.serialNumber`.
Types normalise on parse, so equality is canonical: `Iban.parse('gb82 west ...') == Iban.parse('GB82WEST...')`. Compare parsed values, never the raw strings you parsed them from.
Check-digit types validate the real standard, not a regex shape: IBAN mod-97, card numbers Luhn, ISBN/EAN/ISSN check digits. A value that parses has passed its checksum.

`Percentage` names the unit that a raw double cannot: `Percentage.tryFrom(15)` and `Percentage.tryFromFraction(0.15)` are the same proportion, `.value` holds the percent, `.fraction` the fraction, and `.of(200)` applies it. It is unbounded on purpose (250% growth and -12% churn are real), so finiteness is its only invariant.

Pure Dart with minimal dependencies, so it runs in CLI, server, web and Flutter. Opinionated integrations (JSON, fpdart, Hive, Flutter form validators) are opt-in companion packages, never forced on core consumers.
